finding: There is no live range for this job yet, so this is a first build. Built totals, labor only (no parts), stated hours x $120-$160/hr (the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2015 Hyundai Elantra about $96-$176 (0.8-1.1 hr); midsize 2017 Honda CR-V about $96-$176 (0.8-1.1 hr); truck 2016 Ford F-150 about $132-$202 (1.1-1.26 hr); luxury 2017 Genesis G80 about $108-$176 (0.9-1.1 hr). Across classes that is roughly $96-$202. How this compares: the built range sits squarely on the consumer guides ($100-$200 and $100-$175 for a four-wheel alignment) and on one dealer menu ($139.95-$169.95), and below RepairPal's national average of $186-$273 (F-150 $188-$276, Silverado $166-$243, Accord $157-$231, Camry $223-$326). So the build is about right for a chain or independent shop and somewhat low for a dealer; a shown range of about $100-$250 would cover both. Candidly, an alignment is sold at a menu price, not billed by the hour. Chains often sell it below a book-time build as a coupon item or bundle it with tires, and sell lifetime plans at about the price of two alignments, while dealers and shops that calibrate driver-assist cameras charge above it. Our hours are manufacturer warranty times, the low end of what a shop bills. How solid the labor times are: fair for three classes, weak for trucks. Maker-printed times were found for the midsize example itself (Honda 0.8 hr, 2017-20 CR-V), the luxury example itself (Genesis 1.1 hr, 2017-18 G80) and, through an all-models bulletin, the economy example (Hyundai 1.1 hr). The other end of each range is another maker's figure for a comparable vehicle (Honda 0.8 hr, Tesla 0.90 hr), clearly labelled. For trucks no stated time was found for an F-150, Silverado or Ram: the GM alignment bulletin names its labor operations without printing times, so the truck range rests on Hyundai's all-models 1.1 hr and Tesla's 1.26 hr for a Cybertruck, neither a conventional pickup. Acura's 0.4 hr is an add-on allowance when the car is already apart and Ford's 0.6 hr covers rear toe only; both are cross-checks, not used. Not found: a chain shop's own posted alignment price (the chain pages reached listed none) and an alignment-equipment maker's stated time. A front-only (two-wheel) alignment is a smaller job, about $50-$100 in the guides. Seized adjusters, cam bolts, shims and worn parts are extra, and an alignment cannot be finished on worn tie rods or ball joints. Reviewer note (2026-11-19): the Tesla service-manual figures (0.90 for the Model 3, 1.26 for the Cybertruck) are printed without a unit, so they are kept as cross-checks only and no longer set a range end. Truck and luxury hours are now the single Hyundai/Genesis stated time of 1.1 hr: luxury (2017 Genesis G80, the example itself) builds to about $132-$176 and truck (not a truck-specific time) to about $132-$176.
extras: A quote may add: freeing or replacing seized adjusters, eccentric (cam) bolts or sleeves; camber or caster shims or adjustment kits on vehicles with no factory adjustment; worn tie rod ends, ball joints, bushings or wheel bearings that must be replaced before the alignment will hold; a steering angle sensor reset; calibration of driver-assist cameras or radar on newer vehicles (can cost more than the alignment itself); extra labor for lifted, lowered or modified vehicles; an alignment check or inspection fee if no adjustment is made; shop supplies and sales tax. Lifetime or multi-year alignment plans cost more up front. Ask for the before-and-after printout.
